subject: Advanced begineer R user, wants to know about shell scripting tools.

messages.author: 0a26429513db9cdf
messages.subject: Advanced begineer R user, wants to know about shell scripting tools.
parts:
Hello,

Hope y'all are enjoying your summer.  I have a recently used bash/awk to do some data manipulation using my git bash terminal ( my laptop runs on Windows 10, 4GB RAM).  It was a good feeling since R is the only language I am somewhat comfortable with but splitting 22 million rows of 4-word sentences into one word 4 columns was too memory intense for my laptop. 

After understanding I little bit about how data manipulation in bash this was a very fast procedure using awk in shell.

My inquiry for DRUG is: Since I use Windows I don't have bash shell (Windows 10 is suppose to have developers tools that allows some sort of installation of shell but for some reason it is not working on my computer) and even though git bash did the trick this time I think it lacks full functionality( for one the man command or the sudo(not that i know know how to use it yet) command is not in git bash, thus I was thinking about installing Linux on a Flash drive I have (its 32GB).

Given that I am working in a vacuum, I was hoping to learn about installing and booting off of a USB versus partitioning my hard disk for dual-boot.  What I am trying to get an understanding of is, if I boot off a USB what are the limitations? Is it as useful as having a shell in Mac? How much does it limit me? Is Cygwin something that is better in this case?  Or is it common to just plug away with git bash?  I am trying to at least work like a pro.

I addition I found an online course I planning to go over on Edx.org, 'Introduction to Linux' and they are purposing either USB installation or VM Box Linux client for beginner.

These are some novice questions but I am curious much will I it limit linux's capabilities to boot off a USB.  In future I might want to integrate Hadoop HDFS and R, or other big data technologies, where if I am not wrong I would be working from the command line.  And I would like to transition to a command line user in any case to get away from Windows idiosyncrasies, especially when doing data analysis projects.

Thanks in advance for your time and insight.
Best Regards,
Sher

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Advanced begineer R user, wants to know about shell scripting tools.
parts:
Running Linux from a USB, depending on the installation type consumes
quite a bit of RAM. You don't have much to begin with, so that
experience might not be great. It's quite easy to make a Live Linux usb
and test. As long as you read/write data from your main computer drive
the RAM should be the only big limitation. If you set up a persistent
usb stick which allows software upgrades within linux and saving files
to the stick that will perform even slower. VirtualBox may or may not be
any better considering how much ram you have, but is probably better. It
is by far easier than other options because you can easily redo, or try
different things. Picking a less graphics intensive distro would help,
or if you really want to jump in install a server variant and get no GUI.

I tested Windows Linux subshell installation the other day, following
instructions like
https://answers.microsoft.com/en-us/insider/wiki/insider_wintp-insider_install/how-to-enable-the-windows-subsystem-for-linux/16e8f2e8-4a6a-4325-a89a-fd28c7841775
Talk to your dept IT if you need help.

Considering your hardware I would recommend the following:
1. Get access to a computer cluster on campus, chances are your dept or
advisor belongs to at least once group who has access to one.
2. Use a cloud service, you can get 12 months free use of Amazon AWS
micro instance. Paying for something more to test HDFS etc for a few
minutes/hours at a time won't break the bank. There's even
pre-configured Hadoop deployments.
3. Upgrade the RAM in your laptop, it's probably capable of 8-16 GB of
RAM for $100 or less.

Cygwin is not worth it. I would dual boot before that. Of the local
options dual booting would perform the best but is also the trickiest to
setup (though not usually hard, backup 1st).

If you have more questions, consider the email lists on http://lugod.org
the local linux user group and the #linux channel on
https://ucdavis.slack.com

Enjoy,
Alex Mandel, PhD

Center for Spatial Sciences
http://spatial.ucdavis.edu

http://gfc.ucdavis.edu

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Advanced begineer R user, wants to know about shell scripting tools.
parts:
Hi Sher,

All good points from Alex.

A few other thoughts...do you need to save these files individually, or do additional analysis with them which would summarize them down a bit more? How many times/files do you need to do this?

I ask because if you might be able to try running your tasks in parallel in R, and a laptop could probably accomplish this. It is a memory suck for sure, but working with large files generally is regardless. There's a lot out there on running things in parallel. 

I ran the following code on my laptop and it took a few minutes. It creates a file that's 20 million lines long, and parses the words out as you mention, then writes out to a file that is 150kb in size when using high compression. I do have 16GB of RAM and ran this on a 2015 MBP. Depending on what you are after, you may be able to set your tasks up in parallel.

Also, not sure if you had any luck setting up a Linux subsystem on Windows, but a friend of mine has had good things to say, and was able to set things up using these install instructions here: https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/commandline/wsl/install_guide 


Best of luck!

Adios,
Ryan

###### 

library(tidyverse)

# some data
words<-"dogs hate cats sometimes"

# make into tibble
dat <- tibble(X=rep(words, 20000000))

library(stringr)

# split out words:
dat2<-str_split_fixed(dat$X, pattern = " ", n=4) 

# write to RDS file with highest compression ("xz"):
write_rds(dat2, path = "string_example.rds", compress = "xz")

parts:
Thank you for sharing your knowledge.

After reading and looking into all the options that were shared I am interested in setting up a dual boosting system, thanks for the linux email list as well.

As for what Ryan asked about the nature of my project, I am taking this opportunity to learn to work with data that my machine is having a difficulty handling, and in my first go I was processing everything in chunks but now with bash capabilities in hand and learning about 'tibble' will try to do it elegantly and try to model with the complete set of observations.  I did run your code in my machine and there were no hiccups.  But I have some more testing and playing around to do and might have to come back with more questions.  Just wanted to thank you for your quick feedback.

Also, I gather that Windows 10 subsystem is something worth looking into and will try to set it up ( I believe I have turned off some services in my windows 20 for performance sake that are now interfering with the installation).

Thanks again.
